objectives: Describe the pathophysiology and diagnostic signs of glaucoma, including tonometry and optic-disc cupping.
Differentiate cataract, age-related macular degeneration, and diabetic retinopathy by their mechanisms and findings.
Match each disease to the appropriate diagnostic instrument: slit lamp, OCT, and fundus photography.

slides.title: Glaucoma — pressure, the optic nerve, and cupping
slides.body:
**Glaucoma** is a group of progressive **optic neuropathies** characterised by loss of **retinal ganglion cells** and their axons, producing a distinctive pattern of optic-nerve-head damage and visual-field loss. It is a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. The chief **modifiable risk factor** is elevated **intraocular pressure (IOP)**, though glaucoma can occur at statistically normal pressures (**normal-tension glaucoma**) and high pressure without damage is merely **ocular hypertension**.

The most common form, **primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG)**, arises from **increased resistance to aqueous outflow** at the **trabecular meshwork**, raising IOP per the Goldmann equation $P_o = F/C + P_v$ — a falling outflow facility $C$ drives $P_o$ up. **Angle-closure glaucoma**, by contrast, results from mechanical blockage of the drainage angle by the iris, an ophthalmic emergency when acute. The angle is examined by **gonioscopy** with a mirrored contact lens.

The hallmark structural sign is **optic-disc cupping**. The optic nerve head has a central **cup** within the surrounding pink **neuroretinal rim**; as axons die, the rim thins and the cup enlarges, raising the **cup-to-disc (C/D) ratio**. A C/D ratio above about $0.6$, asymmetry between the two eyes of more than $0.2$, rim notching, or a **disc haemorrhage** are red flags. The rim should normally follow the **ISNT rule** — thickest **I**nferior, then **S**uperior, **N**asal, and thinnest **T**emporal; violation suggests glaucomatous loss.

Functional damage is mapped by **perimetry** (visual-field testing), classically with the **Humphrey Field Analyzer** using **standard automated perimetry**. Characteristic defects respect the horizontal midline and follow the nerve-fibre-layer arrangement: **nasal steps**, **arcuate (Bjerrum) scotomas**, and eventually tunnel vision. Structural loss is quantified by **OCT** measurement of the **retinal nerve fibre layer (RNFL)** thickness, which often precedes detectable field loss.

IOP itself is measured by **tonometry**. The reference standard is **Goldmann applanation tonometry** (after **Hans Goldmann**), based on the **Imbert–Fick law**, but it is biased by **central corneal thickness** — a correction established by the **Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS)**, which also showed that lowering IOP reduces conversion to glaucoma. Treatment lowers IOP with drops (**prostaglandin analogues** such as **latanoprost**, **beta-blockers** such as **timolol**, **carbonic anhydrase inhibitors**), **laser trabeculoplasty**, or surgery (**trabeculectomy**, drainage devices, or **minimally invasive glaucoma surgery, MIGS**).

slides.title: Cataract, age-related macular degeneration, and diabetic retinopathy
slides.body:
Three further diseases dominate the optometric clinic, each striking a different optical or neural structure.

**Cataract** is opacification of the **crystalline lens** — the leading cause of treatable blindness globally. With age, lens proteins (**crystallins**) aggregate and the lens yellows and scatters light, reducing contrast and acuity and causing glare. The classic morphological types are **nuclear sclerotic** (central hardening, which can paradoxically cause a temporary **myopic shift** and 'second sight'), **cortical** (spoke-like wedge opacities), and **posterior subcapsular** (a plaque at the back of the lens that especially degrades near vision and reading). Cataract is diagnosed at the **slit lamp** and graded by systems such as **LOCS III** (Lens Opacities Classification System III). Definitive treatment is surgical: **phacoemulsification** — ultrasonic emulsification of the lens, refined by **Charles Kelman** in 1967 — with implantation of an **intraocular lens (IOL)**.

**Age-related macular degeneration (AMD)** attacks the central **macula** and is a leading cause of irreversible central vision loss in older adults. The earliest sign is **drusen** — yellowish extracellular deposits beneath the **retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)**. **Dry (non-exudative) AMD** progresses slowly to **geographic atrophy**; **wet (neovascular) AMD** features **choroidal neovascularisation** driven by **vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)**, with leakage, haemorrhage, and rapid distortion. Patients self-monitor distortion with the **Amsler grid** (after **Marc Amsler**, 1947). Wet AMD is now treated with intravitreal **anti-VEGF** agents (**ranibizumab**, **aflibercept**, **bevacizumab**); the **AREDS/AREDS2** vitamin formulations slow progression of intermediate dry AMD.

**Diabetic retinopathy (DR)** is a microvascular complication of **diabetes mellitus** and a leading cause of blindness in working-age adults. Chronic hyperglycaemia damages retinal capillaries, producing **microaneurysms**, **dot-and-blot haemorrhages**, **hard exudates**, and **cotton-wool spots** in the **non-proliferative** stage. As ischaemia worsens, VEGF release drives **proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)** — fragile **neovascularisation** that can bleed into the vitreous or cause **tractional retinal detachment**. **Diabetic macular oedema (DME)** — fluid in the macula — is the commonest cause of vision loss in DR at any stage. The grading framework descends from the **Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS)**. Management spans tight **glycaemic control**, **panretinal photocoagulation** laser (a legacy of the **Diabetic Retinopathy Study**), **anti-VEGF** injection, and vitrectomy. Crucially, early DR is **asymptomatic**, which is why regular dilated screening — increasingly automated — is the cornerstone of prevention.

slides.title: The diagnostic toolkit — slit lamp, OCT, and fundus photography
slides.body:
Modern eye diagnosis rests on a handful of powerful instruments, each suited to particular structures and diseases.

The **slit lamp biomicroscope** is the optometrist's workhorse for the **anterior segment**. Invented by **Allvar Gullstrand** (who demonstrated slit illumination in **1911**) and developed into the modern instrument by **Hans Goldmann**, it combines a high-intensity **slit of light** with a **stereo microscope**, letting the examiner sweep an optical section through the transparent cornea, anterior chamber, iris, and lens. Techniques include **direct illumination**, **retroillumination**, and **specular reflection** (to count corneal endothelial cells). With auxiliary lenses (a **Goldmann three-mirror** or a high-plus **78/90 D condensing lens**) the slit lamp also examines the **posterior segment** and optic disc, and it carries the **Goldmann applanation tonometer**.

**Optical coherence tomography (OCT)** is the most transformative imaging advance in modern ophthalmology. Introduced by **David Huang**, **James Fujimoto**, and colleagues at MIT in a landmark **1991** *Science* paper, OCT uses **low-coherence interferometry** — an optical analogue of ultrasound that measures **echo time delay of back-scattered light** with a **Michelson interferometer**. It produces **micron-resolution cross-sections** of the retina *in vivo*, non-invasively. Successive generations — **time-domain**, then **spectral-domain (SD-OCT)**, then **swept-source** — increased speed and depth. OCT quantifies the **retinal nerve fibre layer** and **ganglion cell complex** in glaucoma, images **drusen** and **subretinal fluid** in AMD, and measures **macular thickness** in diabetic macular oedema. **OCT angiography (OCTA)** extends it to map retinal blood flow without dye.

**Fundus photography** documents the **retina, optic disc, and vasculature** in a wide-field colour image, providing an objective, comparable record over time and the substrate for **telemedicine** and **AI screening**. **Fluorescein angiography (FA)** — injecting sodium fluorescein and photographing the dye transit — reveals leakage, ischaemia, and neovascularisation in DR and AMD; **indocyanine green (ICG) angiography** images the deeper choroidal circulation.

The instruments map onto disease. **Glaucoma**: tonometry + disc photography + OCT RNFL + perimetry. **Cataract**: the slit lamp. **AMD**: OCT + fundus photos + Amsler grid + FA for wet disease. **Diabetic retinopathy**: dilated fundus exam, fundus photography (the basis of automated screening such as **IDx-DR**), OCT for macular oedema, and FA for ischaemia and neovascularisation. Choosing the right tool — and reading it accurately — is the diagnostic core of clinical optometry, and increasingly the input layer for the AI systems explored in the final lesson.

question.question: Which set of findings is most characteristic of glaucomatous optic neuropathy?
options: Drusen beneath the RPE, geographic atrophy, and distortion on the Amsler grid.
Increased cup-to-disc ratio with neuroretinal rim thinning, an arcuate visual-field defect, and thinning of the retinal nerve fibre layer on OCT.
Microaneurysms, dot-and-blot haemorrhages, and hard exudates with neovascularisation.
A yellow, light-scattering crystalline lens causing glare and a myopic shift.
question.explanation: Glaucoma is an optic neuropathy: loss of retinal ganglion-cell axons enlarges the optic-disc cup (raised cup-to-disc ratio) and thins the neuroretinal rim, OCT shows retinal nerve fibre layer thinning, and perimetry reveals nerve-fibre-bundle defects such as arcuate (Bjerrum) scotomas and nasal steps. Option A describes age-related macular degeneration, option C describes diabetic retinopathy, and option D describes cataract — none of which are the optic-nerve picture of glaucoma.

hints: Glaucoma damages the optic nerve head and the nerve fibre layer.
Look for cupping, rim thinning, and arcuate field loss.
slides.workedSolution: Glaucoma kills retinal ganglion cells, so the disc cup enlarges, the rim thins (often violating the ISNT rule), the OCT RNFL thins, and the visual field shows arcuate scotomas or nasal steps respecting the horizontal midline. That is the constellation in option B. The other options are AMD (A), diabetic retinopathy (C), and cataract (D).

question.question: An optic disc has a vertical disc diameter of $1.8\,\text{mm}$ and a vertical cup diameter of $1.08\,\text{mm}$. Compute the vertical cup-to-disc ratio to two decimal places.
question.hint: Cup-to-disc ratio = cup diameter / disc diameter = 1.08 / 1.8.

question.question: Which imaging modality uses low-coherence interferometry to produce micron-resolution cross-sectional images of the retina in vivo, and was first reported by Huang, Fujimoto and colleagues in 1991?
question.explanation: Optical coherence tomography (OCT), introduced by David Huang, James Fujimoto and colleagues in a 1991 Science paper, uses low-coherence interferometry (a Michelson interferometer) to measure the echo time delay of back-scattered light, building micron-resolution cross-sections of the retina non-invasively. Fundus photography (option A) gives a colour surface image, not a cross-section. Goldmann applanation tonometry (option C) measures intraocular pressure, and gonioscopy (option D) visualises the drainage angle — neither produces tomographic retinal images.

hints: It is the optical analogue of ultrasound for the retina.
slides.workedSolution: OCT (Huang, Fujimoto et al., Science 1991) applies low-coherence interferometry — measuring the time delay and intensity of back-scattered light with a Michelson interferometer — to generate cross-sectional, micron-resolution images of the retina in vivo. That is option B; the others measure pressure, the angle, or a surface photo.

question.question: A diabetic patient with 20/20 vision asks why annual dilated screening matters
question.prompt: A 52-year-old with 12 years of type 2 diabetes has 20/20 vision and no symptoms, and questions why you insist on an annual dilated fundus exam and retinal photographs. Using the natural history of diabetic retinopathy — from microaneurysms and haemorrhages through ischaemia, VEGF-driven proliferative neovascularisation, and diabetic macular oedema — explain why sight-threatening disease can be present while vision is still normal, what specific findings the dilated exam and fundus photography are looking for, and how OCT contributes when macular oedema is suspected. Conclude with why early detection changes the outcome.

question.question: Wet (neovascular) age-related macular degeneration is driven by choroidal neovascularisation. Which class of treatment most directly targets its underlying mechanism?
options: Prostaglandin-analogue eye drops to lower intraocular pressure.
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections such as ranibizumab or aflibercept.
Panretinal photocoagulation of the peripheral retina.
question.explanation: Wet AMD is driven by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), which stimulates leaky choroidal neovascular membranes under the macula. Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents (ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab) block that signal directly and are the standard of care. Prostaglandin drops (option A) treat glaucoma by lowering IOP; phacoemulsification with an IOL (option C) treats cataract; panretinal photocoagulation (option D) is a treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy, not the choroidal neovascularisation of AMD.

hints: What molecule drives the abnormal new vessels in wet AMD?
The therapy is injected into the vitreous and blocks a growth factor.
slides.workedSolution: Choroidal neovascularisation in wet AMD is stimulated by VEGF. Blocking VEGF with intravitreal injections of ranibizumab, aflibercept, or bevacizumab directly addresses the mechanism and is the standard treatment. Option B is correct; the others treat glaucoma, cataract, or proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
